items.question: You call event.stopPropagation() inside a listener attached to the target element itself. Another listener for the same event is registered on the same element afterward. Does it still run? What changes if you used stopImmediatePropagation() instead?
items.answer: With stopPropagation(), other listeners on the same element still run; it only stops propagation to other nodes. stopImmediatePropagation() also prevents the remaining listeners on the same element from firing. Neither re-enables propagation once stopped.
items.trap: The naive answer treats them as interchangeable or assumes stopPropagation() blocks sibling listeners. It doesn't: only stopImmediatePropagation() stops listeners on the same target. This matters when a component's own handler must preempt other handlers on the same node.

items.question: Your delegated handler on a <ul> does const btn = event.target.closest('[data-id]') and uses btn directly. A click lands on a <span> whose closest('[data-id]') matches a button that lives outside the list (e.g., a toolbar button that is an ancestor of the list). What's the bug and the fix?
items.answer: Verify the match is inside the delegated root with `if (!btn || !list.contains(btn)) return;`. closest() walks up the ancestor chain and can match an element outside the subtree you delegated on, so without the contains() guard you may act on unrelated elements.
items.trap: The naive answer assumes closest() is scoped to the delegated container. It isn't; it climbs to document, so a selector matching an ancestor outside the list yields a false positive. The list.contains(btn) check is what keeps delegation correct.

items.question: A cookie is set with HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax. Can your JavaScript read its value through document.cookie?
items.answer: No. HttpOnly makes the cookie inaccessible to JavaScript (document.cookie cannot read or set it); it is only sent in HTTP requests. Secure restricts it to HTTPS transport and SameSite controls cross-site sending, but neither makes it JS-readable.
items.trap: The naive answer conflates 'sent to the server' with 'readable from JS'. HttpOnly exists precisely to keep tokens (e.g., session cookies) out of XSS-reachable JavaScript. If you need a value in JS, it cannot be the HttpOnly auth cookie.

items.question: You store a draft in sessionStorage and expect the second tab the user opens to see it. It doesn't. Why, and what's the one case where a new tab does start with that data?
items.answer: sessionStorage is scoped to a single browsing context (tab), so two independently opened tabs do not share it and it's cleared when the tab closes. The exception is duplicating a tab (e.g., 'duplicate tab' or a link opened from the page): the new copy is seeded with the source tab's sessionStorage.
items.trap: The naive answer treats sessionStorage as 'localStorage but temporary and shared'. It is per-tab, not shared across tabs, so it's the wrong choice for cross-tab state; use localStorage, IndexedDB, or a BroadcastChannel for that.

items.question: You abort a fetch with controller.abort() and catch the rejection in the same catch block you use for network errors, then show the user an error toast. What's wrong, and how do you tell an intentional abort from a real failure?
items.answer: An abort is expected, not an error to surface. Distinguish it by checking signal.aborted or error.name === 'AbortError' (DOMException) before treating the rejection as a failure; only report/log the rest. Often the cleanest pattern is to rethrow the AbortError or let it be swallowed by the caller that initiated the abort.
items.trap: The naive answer catches all rejections uniformly. Conflating abort with failure spams error logs and shows users error UI for navigations or unmounts they themselves triggered, a very common bug in React effects that fetch on prop change.

items.question: You do const data = await response.json(); and later await response.json(); again to log the raw body. What happens, and what's the safe way to read the body twice?
items.answer: The second call rejects: a Response body is a ReadableStream consumed once, and after the first read it is locked/used. To read it twice, call response.clone() before the first read and read from the clone, or tee the stream. Cloning copies the body and has a cost, so avoid it in hot paths.
items.trap: The naive answer assumes response.json() is a cheap getter you can call repeatedly. It's a one-shot stream consumption. The same trap applies to text(), arrayBuffer(), and blob(); mixing reads on one Response throws.

items.question: You caches.open('v1').then(c => c.put(req, res)) a Response whose headers include Cache-Control: no-store, max-age=0. Will the Cache API refuse to store it or evict it after max-age?
items.answer: No. The Cache API is script-controlled storage of Request/Response pairs; it does not interpret or enforce HTTP cache directives. put() stores whatever you give it, and entries stay until your code deletes them or the origin's storage is evicted. You must implement your own expiration, versioning, and invalidation.
items.trap: The naive answer assumes the Cache API behaves like the HTTP cache and honors Cache-Control. It doesn't; no-store won't prevent put, and max-age won't evict. Treating the Cache API as 'HTTP cache I control' leads to stale or leaked data.

items.question: Your service worker caches a navigation to '/' and, separately, an XHR GET '/' that returns JSON. Both use the default cache.match(request). Why might they collide, and what determines the cache key?
items.answer: By default the Cache API matches on the request URL and method (and, depending on ignoreSearch/ignoreVary, the query string and the Vary header). Two different Request objects to the same URL+method are the same entry, so a navigation and an API call to '/' can overwrite each other. Use distinct URLs, keep ignoreVary false, and be deliberate with ignoreSearch.
items.trap: The naive answer thinks the cache key is the Request object identity or that different fetch calls get different entries. The key is URL+method, so unrelated requests to the same URL collide, a classic cause of serving JSON where HTML was expected.

items.question: You worker.postMessage(buffer) an ArrayBuffer and immediately read buffer.byteLength on the main thread afterwards. It's 0. Why, and what did you actually want?
items.answer: If you passed the buffer in the transfer list (postMessage(data, [buffer])), ownership moved to the worker and the original is detached (byteLength becomes 0). Without a transfer list it's copied and the original stays intact. Transfer is zero-copy but one-way for that buffer; pick it only when you won't need the data on the sender side.
items.trap: The naive answer assumes 'postMessage copies everything, so the original is fine' or 'transfer is just an optimization with no side effects'. Transferables are detached on the sender; using them like a copy silently empties your buffer.

items.question: You send { type: 'run', fn: (x) => x * 2 } to a worker via postMessage. It throws. Why, and what's the correct pattern?
items.answer: Functions are not structured-cloneable, so postMessage throws a DataCloneError. The same applies to DOM nodes, Window, and non-transferable objects held by reference. Send a serializable command (e.g., { type: 'run', op: 'double' }) and let the worker own the implementation; the worker maps the command to a function it already has.
items.trap: The naive answer assumes structured clone is deep equality for any value. It isn't; it covers primitives, plain objects, arrays, Maps/Sets, Date, Blob, ArrayBuffer, etc., but not functions or DOM. Trying to ship behavior across the boundary fails at runtime.

items.question: In a ResizeObserver callback you set entry.target.style.width = entry.contentRect.width + 10 + 'px'. The page jitters or freezes. What's happening and how do you fix it?
items.answer: Changing the observed element's size inside the callback schedules another resize observation, which can loop. Guard with a condition that stops when the size is already correct, debounce the write, or move the mutation to a non-observed element. ResizeObserver also batches, so iterate all entries and avoid unbounded layout writes.
items.trap: The naive answer treats the callback like a one-shot event. Resizing the observed element in its own callback is a feedback loop; the browser keeps re-observing the change. This is the classic ResizeObserver-induced layout thrash.

items.question: You call observer.observe(el) on an element that is already in the viewport. You expect the callback to fire only when it scrolls out and back in. What actually happens?
items.answer: An initial entry is delivered asynchronously shortly after observe(), with isIntersecting reflecting the current state. Observers don't wait for a change to fire; they report the current condition first. Write the callback to handle an initial entry (e.g., lazy-load immediately if already visible) rather than assuming it only fires on transitions.
items.trap: The naive answer assumes observers fire only on change. They deliver an initial batch, so code that 'starts' work in the callback can run for already-visible elements; fine if expected, a double-load bug if not.

items.question: On first visit you call navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js') and immediately try to use a feature that requires the SW to control the page. It fails. Why, and how do you coordinate correctly?
items.answer: A newly registered service worker installs but does not control the page that registered it until a later navigation or reload. Use navigator.serviceWorker.ready (resolves when an active SW controls the page) or listen for controllerchange before relying on control. On first load the page is controlled by no SW or by the previous one.
items.trap: The naive answer equates 'registered' with 'in control now'. Registration only starts the lifecycle; the current page is still uncontrolled until activation plus navigation. Assuming control after register is a top cause of 'works after refresh, not on first visit' bugs.

items.question: To make updates instant you call self.skipWaiting() in the install handler and clients.claim() in activate. Users report broken UI right after a deploy. What went wrong?
items.answer: skipWaiting() makes the new SW control open clients immediately, but if your assets aren't content-hashed and versioned, the page may now be served by a SW whose caches don't match the HTML/JS it's running, mixing versions. Only skipWaiting when assets are versioned and the page can tolerate the new SW; otherwise let the new SW wait and activate on next navigation.
items.trap: The naive answer treats skipWaiting as a free 'update fast' flag. It's a version-consistency hazard: the new SW takes over mid-session, so the running page can request assets the new caches don't have. Without content hashing, this ships broken UI.

items.question: navigator.storage.estimate() reports usage/quota = 0.4. You write 100 MB and assume it fits because you're under quota. The write throws a quota error. Why?
items.answer: estimate() is approximate and best-effort, not a reservation; the real available space depends on disk, other origins, and browser policy, and can change between the estimate and the write. Treat it as guidance for pruning, and always try/catch writes with a recovery/sync path. Never build correctness around a remembered number.
items.trap: The naive answer treats estimate() like a filesystem statvfs guarantee. It's an estimate that can be stale and inaccurate, and eviction can occur concurrently. Code that 'checks quota then writes without catching' fails in production.

items.question: You call navigator.storage.persist() and it resolves true. Can you now stop syncing user data to the server because local storage is permanent?
items.answer: No. persist() reduces the chance of automatic eviction under pressure and persisted() reports that state, but it is not a durability guarantee: users can clear site data, browsers can enforce policy, and disk failures happen. Persist lowers eviction priority; it doesn't replace server authority or a recovery path.
items.trap: The naive answer reads 'persistent' as 'permanent and safe as the server'. It only changes eviction priority. Treating local storage as the source of truth after persist() loses data when users clear storage or switch devices.

items.question: navigator.permissions.query({ name: 'geolocation' }) returns state: 'granted'. You skip calling getCurrentPosition and try to read cached coordinates. Nothing happens. Why?
items.answer: query() reports permission state; it doesn't grant access or return data. You still must call the capability API (getCurrentPosition/watchPosition), which may require a user gesture and can still fail. Use query() to adapt UI (e.g., disable a button when denied), then request access inside the feature flow.
items.trap: The naive answer conflates 'permission granted' with 'data available'. The Permissions API is a status query, not an accessor. Skipping the capability call means you never actually access the feature.

items.question: At app startup you cache permissionStatus.state as 'granted' and never re-check. The user revokes the permission in browser settings and returns. Your app still tries to use the feature and fails silently. What should you have done?
items.answer: Permission state is not permanent. Listen to the PermissionStatus change event and re-query when the user returns to the tab (e.g., on visibilitychange), because settings can change outside your app. Update UI and capability availability from the latest state, not a cached snapshot.
items.trap: The naive answer treats a grant as sticky for the session. Permissions can be revoked in OS/browser settings at any time, so a cached 'granted' becomes a lie. The change event and re-query on focus are what keep the UI honest.

items.question: You call indexedDB.open('app', 3) to run a migration, but a tab still has version 1 open. onupgradeneeded never fires. What's happening, and what events must you handle?
items.answer: A version-change transaction requires that no other connection holds an older version; the open is blocked and onblocked fires. The other tab must close its connection (it receives versionchange) so the upgrade can proceed. Handle onblocked to prompt the user, and listen for versionchange on open connections to close and reopen cooperatively.
items.trap: The naive answer assumes open(v3) upgrades immediately. It can't while another tab holds the DB; it blocks. Forgetting onblocked/versionchange is why multi-tab migrations 'hang' in production.

items.question: You want to add an index at runtime, so inside a normal readwrite transaction you call store.createIndex(...). It throws. Why, and where must schema changes happen?
items.answer: Creating or deleting object stores and indexes is only allowed inside the version-change transaction that runs during onupgradeneeded. Runtime readwrite/readonly transactions can only read and mutate records. Bump the DB version and do structural work in the upgrade transaction.
items.trap: The naive answer treats IndexedDB like a SQL DB where you can ALTER anytime. Structural operations are restricted to the upgrade transaction; attempting them in a normal transaction throws, so 'add an index lazily' isn't a valid pattern.

items.question: Your service worker uses cache-first for /api/me, which returns the signed-in user's profile. A shared device user logs out, and the next user sees the previous user's profile. What's the root cause and the rule?
items.answer: Authenticated or personalized responses must not be cached without a deliberate per-user keying and security design. Cache-first served a stale, personalized body across sessions. Use network-only (or network-first with no caching) for authenticated endpoints, key caches by user, and clear personalized caches on logout.
items.trap: The naive answer thinks 'cache-first is fast and fine for GETs'. For personalized data it leaks one user's data to another. Caching /api/me without per-user keys is a security bug, not just a staleness bug.

items.question: You serve app.js (unhashed filename) with stale-while-revalidate. You ship a bugfix, but users keep reporting the old behavior for days. Why isn't SWR updating them?
items.answer: SWR returns the cached response immediately and updates in the background, but with an unhashed filename the cached entry and the network response share a key, and long-lived tabs may never pick up the update; the SW itself may also serve the old app.js from cache. Content-hash your filenames (app.<hash>.js) so new content is a new cache key, and version the precache list.
items.trap: The naive answer assumes SWR guarantees freshness. It only revalidates; without content-addressed filenames, stale code can persist across sessions. Immutable, hashed assets are what make cache strategies safe.

items.question: You share state across tabs with localStorage and listen for the storage event, expecting your service worker to receive it and refresh its cache. It never does. Why?
items.answer: Web Storage (localStorage/sessionStorage) and its storage event are only available in window contexts; service workers (and dedicated workers) cannot access them, so the SW never gets the event. Use BroadcastChannel (which reaches workers) or have a tab call postMessage to the SW, and keep durable data in IndexedDB/Cache API.
items.trap: The naive answer treats localStorage + the storage event as a general cross-context bus. It's window-only, so the SW is deaf to it. This is why the bank says avoid localStorage as a cross-context database.

items.question: Two tabs edit the same note and each broadcasts note-changed via BroadcastChannel; every tab re-reads from IndexedDB on the message. Tab A's write lands after Tab B's, overwriting it. Did BroadcastChannel keep the data consistent?
items.answer: No. BroadcastChannel is a fire-and-forget notification, not a transaction, lock, or conflict-resolution mechanism. Concurrent writes can race and last-write-wins can lose data. You need server authority, versioning/ETag checks, or an explicit coordination protocol; messages only signal 're-read', they don't serialize writes.
items.trap: The naive answer assumes broadcasting a change event is enough for consistency. It isn't; messages have no delivery guarantees and no ordering across concurrent writers. Treating BroadcastChannel as a conflict resolver causes silent data loss.

mcqs.question: A button has two click listeners registered with addEventListener. The first calls event.stopPropagation(). The page also has a click listener on document.body. Which listeners still run?
options: Only the button's first listener runs; the second and the body listener are both blocked.
Both the button's second listener and the body listener run.
The button's second listener runs, but the body listener does not.
Neither the button's second listener nor the body listener runs, and an error is thrown.
mcqs.explanation: stopPropagation() prevents the event from moving to other nodes (so body never receives it), but it does not stop other listeners on the same target; the button's second listener still runs. Only stopImmediatePropagation() blocks sibling listeners on the same element. The strongest distractor claims both same-element listeners and the body listener are blocked, which is exactly what stopImmediatePropagation does, not stopPropagation. No error is thrown.

mcqs.question: Which statement about client-side storage and worker contexts is correct?
options: localStorage and sessionStorage are unavailable in service workers; durable data there must use IndexedDB or the Cache API.
A service worker can read localStorage and sessionStorage but cannot write cookies.
IndexedDB is only available on the main thread, not in dedicated workers or service workers.
sessionStorage is shared across all same-origin tabs so it's ideal for cross-tab state.
mcqs.explanation: Web Storage is synchronous and exposed only in window contexts; service workers (and dedicated workers) cannot access localStorage/sessionStorage, so durable data in those contexts must use IndexedDB or the Cache API. The strongest distractor claims the SW can read Web Storage, the common 'all storage is storage' misconception. Another distractor says sessionStorage is shared across tabs; it's per-tab, not shared. IndexedDB is in fact available in workers.

mcqs.question: You call const res = await fetch('/api/x') and the server responds 500 Internal Server Error. What is the state of res, and what must you check?
options: fetch rejects with an error; wrap in try/catch and that's enough.
fetch fulfills, and res.ok is true because a response was received.
fetch rejects only for 5xx statuses; 4xx statuses fulfill.
fetch fulfills with a Response; you must check res.ok (or res.status) before using the body.
mcqs.explanation: fetch rejects only for network-level failures or aborts; any HTTP status (404, 500) still produces a fulfilled Response, so you must check res.ok/res.status before parsing. The strongest distractor says a try/catch alone is enough, the classic mistake of treating HTTP errors as rejections, which silently swallows server errors. Another distractor claims 5xx rejects but 4xx fulfills; both actually fulfill.

mcqs.question: Inside a service worker you do cache.put(req, res) where res has Cache-Control: no-store. What happens?
options: The Cache API refuses to store the response because of no-store.
The response is stored and remains until your code deletes it or origin storage is evicted.
The response is stored but auto-evicted after max-age seconds.
The Cache API throws a DataCloneError.
mcqs.explanation: The Cache API is script-controlled storage of Request/Response pairs and does not interpret HTTP cache directives; put() stores the response regardless of Cache-Control, and entries persist until your code removes them or origin storage is evicted. The strongest distractor says no-store prevents storage, projecting HTTP-cache semantics onto the Cache API. Another claims auto-eviction after max-age; there is none.

mcqs.question: On the main thread: const buf = new ArrayBuffer(8); worker.postMessage({ buf }, [buf]); console.log(buf.byteLength); What is logged?
options: undefined
It throws a DataCloneError.
mcqs.explanation: Passing buf in the transfer list transfers ownership to the worker; the original ArrayBuffer is detached and its byteLength becomes 0. The strongest distractor logs 8, assuming postMessage always copies, true only without a transfer list. Another says it throws DataCloneError; ArrayBuffer is transferable, so no error.

mcqs.question: A ResizeObserver callback does entry.target.style.width = entry.contentRect.width + 5 + 'px' on every entry. The element flickers/jitters. What's the cause and fix?
options: The observer fires too often; throttle with setTimeout and the loop is harmless.
Resizing the observed element inside its own callback creates a feedback loop; guard so the write stops once the target size is reached, or move the side effect off the observed element.
ResizeObserver doesn't support width changes; switch to MutationObserver.
The callback must return a Promise or the browser retries it.
mcqs.explanation: Mutating the observed element's size in the callback schedules another observation, producing a feedback loop (layout thrash). The fix is a guard that stops when the size is already correct, or moving the write to a non-observed element. The strongest distractor blames frequency and recommends throttling; that masks but doesn't remove the loop. The others invent nonexistent behaviors (switching to MutationObserver, returning a Promise).

mcqs.question: On a first visit you run navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js') and, in the same script, assume the page is now controlled by the SW. What's true?
options: The SW controls the registering page immediately after register() resolves.
The SW controls the page only after the user grants a permission.
register() throws if no SW exists yet.
The newly registered SW installs but does not control the current page until a later navigation; use navigator.serviceWorker.ready or controllerchange to coordinate.
mcqs.explanation: A newly registered SW installs and, after activation, controls pages opened afterward, not the page that registered it. navigator.serviceWorker.ready resolves when an active SW controls the page, or listen for controllerchange. The strongest distractor says the SW controls the registering page immediately, the classic 'works after refresh, breaks on first visit' bug. No permission is needed to register, and register() does not throw on first use.

mcqs.question: navigator.storage.estimate() reports 40% used. Which conclusion is safe?
options: The next write under 60% of quota is guaranteed to succeed.
estimate() reserves the reported usage so it cannot be evicted.
The estimate is approximate guidance; writes can still fail, so catch quota errors and keep data recoverable/synced.
Once usage exceeds 50%, the browser automatically clears IndexedDB.
mcqs.explanation: estimate() is best-effort and approximate, not a reservation or guarantee; available space can change between the estimate and the write, and eviction can occur. Always try/catch writes with a recovery/sync path. The strongest distractor treats the estimate as a hard guarantee that writes under quota will succeed, a dangerous production bug. The others invent reservation and auto-clear behaviors the API doesn't have.

mcqs.question: navigator.permissions.query({ name: 'geolocation' }) returns state: 'granted'. What can you correctly conclude?
options: You can now read the user's location without any further call.
The permission will remain granted until your app revokes it.
The permission is granted; you still must call getCurrentPosition (often from a user gesture) to actually obtain coordinates, and it can still fail.
query() itself triggers the browser permission prompt.
mcqs.explanation: The Permissions API reports state; it doesn't return data or grant access. You still call the capability API (getCurrentPosition), which may require a user gesture and can fail. The strongest distractor says you can read location without any further call, conflating permission with access. Another says the grant is permanent until the app revokes it; permissions can be revoked outside the app, so listen for change. query() never triggers a prompt.

mcqs.question: You need to add a new index to an existing IndexedDB object store. Where must this happen?
options: In any readwrite transaction on that store.
In a readonly transaction after closing and reopening the DB.
Indexes can be added lazily via store.createIndex() in any transaction; no version bump is needed.
Inside the onupgradeneeded version-change transaction, after opening with a higher version.
mcqs.explanation: Creating or deleting object stores and indexes is only permitted in the version-change transaction that runs during onupgradeneeded; open the DB with a higher version to trigger it. The strongest distractor says you can do it in any readwrite transaction, the SQL-style ALTER misconception; createIndex there throws. readonly transactions can't do structural work either, and 'lazy add without a version bump' isn't a valid pattern.

scenarios.prompt: A React effect fetches a user when userId changes and aborts on cleanup. Review the code and identify the bugs.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Three problems. (1) HTTP errors are swallowed: fetch does not reject on 4xx/5xx, so a 404 or 500 silently calls setUser with an error body (or res.json() throws on a non-JSON error page). Check res.ok (or res.status) before parsing. (2) Aborts are reported as errors: when userId changes or the component unmounts, controller.abort() rejects the fetch with an AbortError; the catch shows the user an error toast for a navigation they initiated. Distinguish abort from failure with `if (err.name === 'AbortError') return;` before setError. (3) No guard against setting state after unmount if a non-aborted rejection races with cleanup; the abort check covers the fetch, but any post-.then work should also be defensive. A correct version: `if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + res.status);` then `const user = await res.json();`, and in catch, `if (err.name === 'AbortError' || controller.signal.aborted) return;` before surfacing.
rubric: Identifies that fetch does not reject on HTTP error statuses and that res.ok must be checked before parsing.
Identifies that controller.abort() produces an AbortError that must be distinguished from real failures, not shown to the user.
Notes the risk of calling setUser/setError after unmount and the need for an abort-aware guard.
Proposes a corrected control flow (check ok, parse, branch on AbortError) rather than just adding a generic try/catch.

scenarios.prompt: This service worker fetch handler uses cache-first for everything. Identify the hazards and refactor to a per-resource strategy.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Hazards: (1) Cache-first for everything serves stale HTML/data and breaks correctness for non-versioned assets; (2) it caches authenticated/personalized responses (e.g., /api/me) and can leak one user's data to another on shared devices; (3) a single 'v1' cache with no size bound or cleanup grows unbounded; (4) caching everything regardless of method/headers can store POSTs or opaque responses unintentionally; (5) no failure path when both cache and network miss. Refactor by routing per resource: immutable hashed assets to cache-first; navigations/HTML to network-first falling back to a cached shell offline; API data that may be briefly stale to stale-while-revalidate; authenticated endpoints to network-only (never cache without per-user keying). Add a `event.request.method === 'GET'` guard, versioned caches (e.g., assets-v2), bounded cleanup in activate, and a network-only branch for /api/me. Route on event.request.destination or URL, and only cache.put for safe, public, GET responses.
rubric: Identifies that cache-first-for-everything serves stale content and is wrong for non-versioned assets.
Flags the security hazard of caching authenticated/personalized responses without per-user keying.
Proposes per-resource routing (cache-first for hashed assets, network-first for HTML, SWR for staleable data, network-only for auth).
Adds guards: GET-only, versioned caches, bounded cleanup, and a fallback when cache and network both fail.
Avoids a single global strategy; reasons about failure cost and freshness per resource.

scenarios.prompt: This IndexedDB open is meant to run a v2 migration that adds an index. In production, some users with two tabs open report the migration never completes. Find the bug and fix it.
scenarios.modelAnswer: The migration can't run while another tab holds an open connection to v1: the version-change transaction is blocked and onupgradeneeded never fires until that tab closes its connection. The code handles neither onblocked nor versionchange. Fix: (1) add req.onblocked to surface a 'please close other tabs' message; (2) on every open connection, listen for db.onversionchange and close the connection so the waiting upgrade can proceed, then reopen; (3) don't return req.result from onsuccess synchronously; open is async, so resolve a promise in onsuccess and reject in onerror; (4) keep migrations idempotent and backward-aware (the contains guards are good). Also handle onerror and quota failures. The pattern: open, on versionchange close + notify, on blocked wait/retry, on upgradeneeded do schema work, on success resolve the db.
rubric: Identifies that a held v1 connection in another tab blocks the v2 upgrade and onupgradeneeded won't fire.
Adds onblocked to inform the user and versionchange to close/reopen cooperatively.
Recognizes indexedDB.open is async and the synchronous `return req.result` is wrong; uses a Promise.
Keeps migrations idempotent (the contains guards) and handles onerror/quota.
Describes a multi-tab coordination UX (prompt to close/reopen) rather than hanging silently.

scenarios.prompt: This cross-tab sync uses localStorage + the storage event and expects the service worker to refresh its cache when a note changes. It also assumes the broadcast is enough for consistency. Identify the issues and refactor.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Issues: (1) localStorage and the storage event are window-only; the service worker never receives the event, so its cache isn't refreshed; (2) localStorage is synchronous and a poor cross-context database, and it isn't available in workers; (3) broadcasting a change is a notification, not conflict resolution; two tabs editing the same note race and last-write-wins can lose data; (4) storing the note body in localStorage duplicates durable state that belongs in IndexedDB. Refactor: keep the authoritative note in IndexedDB (accessible from tabs and the SW); use BroadcastChannel('notes') to broadcast an invalidation signal { type: 'note-changed', id, version } that both tabs and the SW listen to; on the message, re-read the note from IndexedDB (or the server) rather than trusting a payload; for concurrent writes, use server authority + version/ETag checks or an explicit coordination protocol; close the channel on teardown. Messages are fire-and-forget, so handlers must be idempotent and re-read durable state.
rubric: Identifies that localStorage/the storage event are window-only and the SW never receives them.
Switches durable state to IndexedDB and signaling to BroadcastChannel, which reaches workers.
Recognizes that a broadcast is a notification, not conflict resolution, and addresses concurrent writes (versioning/server authority).
Makes handlers idempotent and re-reads durable state after the signal rather than trusting the message payload.
Closes the channel on teardown and separates authoritative server state from durable client state and disposable caches.
